securityReviewCheckpoint.enumerationResistance: Independently verified: unknown email, wrong password, missing credential, disabled user, and policy-invalid passwords all produce byte-identical status, headers and body. securityReviewCheckpoint.credentialVersionFinding: passwordChangedAt is PostgreSQL timestamp(3) and JavaScript Date is also millisecond, so the accepted previous+1 arithmetic is not truncated. However a credential row that is deleted and recreated can legitimately reuse a timestamp, so the timestamp is not a unique version counter. A live probe reproduced exactly that: delete and recreate the credential with a different password but the original passwordChangedAt, and the timestamp comparison alone passes while the digest has changed. The in-lock check was therefore strengthened to compare a SHA-256 fingerprint of the stored digest alongside the timestamp.
securityReviewCheckpoint.digestExposure: The Argon2id digest is never returned by verifyCredentialVersioned and never compared in the clear; a one-way SHA-256 fingerprint is returned instead and is never logged. A regression test asserts the stored digest does not appear anywhere in the value the caller receives.
securityReviewCheckpoint.lockKeyFinding: Password reset originally carried its own inline pg_advisory_xact_lock expression rather than the shared helper, duplicating the key derivation in two places where they could drift. It now calls the same helper, so the key exists in exactly one place.
securityReviewCheckpoint.advisoryLockVerified: Login and reset acquire the identical lock key on the same transaction client that performs their protected writes; Argon2id runs before the lock; credential revalidation, session insertion, credential replacement, and session revocation all occur under it; xact-scope releases on rollback; no process-local mutex is used; the accepted createSession signature is retained; and the requirement that future session-creation paths participate is documented.
negativeControls: Disabling the advisory lock and the revalidation makes the critical race test fail with the login resolving successfully.
Removing only the digest fingerprint while keeping the timestamp comparison makes two credential-version tests fail, including the recycled-timestamp case.

acceptedGuarantees.sharedAdvisoryLock: Login and password reset acquire the same transaction-scoped pg_advisory_xact_lock(hashtextextended(user_id, 0)) on the same transaction client that performs their protected writes. The key derivation exists in exactly one shared helper.
acceptedGuarantees.argon2OutsideLock: Argon2id verification runs outside the lock, so a 64 MiB three-iteration allocation is never held under it and concurrent logins are not serialised by hashing.
acceptedGuarantees.loginRevalidatesUnderLock: Login revalidates the credential under the lock before session creation, comparing both passwordChangedAt and a SHA-256 fingerprint of the stored digest. The digest itself is never returned and never logged.
acceptedGuarantees.atomicReset: Password replacement, recovery-token consumption, outstanding-token invalidation, and session revocation are atomic in one transaction: all commit or all roll back.
acceptedGuarantees.inflightRequestsNotCanceled: A password reset does not cancel an HTTP request that was already authorized. Revocation affects subsequent validation only.
acceptedGuarantees.broaderConcurrencyNotClaimed: No concurrency guarantee beyond the above is claimed.

API_RATE_LIMIT_HMAC_SECRET.purpose: HMAC-SHA256 key for deriving rate-limit keys. Not authentication material: authorises nothing, is never sent to a client, never logged.

algorithm.kind: atomic multi-dimensional Redis token bucket with reservation and refund
algorithm.allOrNothing: A request is admitted only when every dimension has capacity, and nothing is written unless every dimension admits.
algorithm.commitAndCheckSuperseded: The pre-hardening design used commit:false on the failure-metered dimensions so that admission wrote nothing and the charge happened after the handler returned. That is retained here as history and was found to be a real concurrent bypass; see concurrentBypassFinding.
algorithm.reservationAndRefund: The committed design reserves a token on every metered dimension at admission, inside the same indivisible script as the check, and refunds it afterwards unless the outcome was a credential failure. AUTHENTICATION_FAILED and RECOVERY_TOKEN_INVALID keep the reservation; every other outcome refunds it. The global workload budget is never refunded.
algorithm.timeSource: Redis TIME, never the caller, so all instances refill identically regardless of local clock skew.
algorithm.noIncrThenExpireRace: The script that creates a key also sets its expiry, so no crash can leave a key without a TTL.
algorithm.keySlot: Every key carries the {tsms-rl} hash tag, keeping a multi-key script inside one cluster slot.
algorithm.refundIsNotIncr: The refund script recomputes refill from Redis TIME and clamps to capacity. It is never an unconditional INCR, it cannot resurrect an expired key, and it cannot mint budget.

guaranteesClaimed: Concurrent requests cannot exceed the configured allowance: the reservation check and the write are one indivisible script step.
No partial writes: a refused request reserves nothing on any dimension.
A legitimate success is refunded, so a valid attempt costs no observable budget.
A failed credential attempt keeps its charge.
Refunds are clamped to capacity and saturating, so duplicate or repeated refunds cannot inflate a bucket.
A refund cannot restore another subject's budget, because keys are HMAC-derived and never caller-selectable.
A key expires after exactly its window, which is also its time to refill to capacity.
Key cardinality is bounded by distinct subjects within one window.
All state is in Redis, so enforcement is total across API instances.
guaranteesNotClaimed: A refund that cannot be written is lost rather than queued or retried, which can under-charge a subject.
Redis Cluster is designed for via the hash tag but was not exercised against a Cluster instance.

concurrentBypassFinding.defect: Admission for the failure-metered dimensions was a check that wrote nothing, with the charge applied after the handler returned. Because those two steps were not atomic, N simultaneous requests all read the same untouched bucket and were all admitted.
concurrentBypassFinding.demonstration: Written against real Redis before the fix, and retained in apps/api/tests/rate-limit-concurrency.integration.test.mjs: 20 concurrent failed logins were all admitted against an allowance of 8; 20 concurrent invalid resets were all admitted against an allowance of 10; the same burst split across two API instances was all admitted.
concurrentBypassFinding.sequentialControl: Sequential traffic correctly refused at the limit, proving the bypass was concurrency-specific and distributed rather than a broken policy.
concurrentBypassFinding.regressionTest: apps/api/tests/rate-limit-concurrency.integration.test.mjs preserves the before evidence and asserts the corrected behaviour of admitting exactly the allowance.

argon2idSemaphore.holderIdentity: 43-character base64url value from 32 random bytes, never derived from a credential, address, or token
coveredWork: login decoy verification for an unknown account
password-recovery decoy verification for an ineligible request
argon2idSemaphore.guarantee: At most 8 valid leases may exist across the whole deployment at one time, and every Argon2id allocation is bracketed by a lease.
argon2idSemaphore.guaranteeNotClaimed: This is NOT an unconditional maximum of 8 physically running Argon2id operations. A lease that expires while its work is still running permits over-admission, bounded by the number of such holders rather than by request volume.
argon2idSemaphore.refusal: Immediate, with no queue and no unlimited fallback. Redis unavailability refuses admission.

policies.globalArgon2idBudget: 120 per 1 minute, one key for the whole deployment, charged before the handler runs
policies.tuning: Frozen source constants, not environment variables. An operator who can raise a limit can also disable the control.
policies.rationale: Conservative development defaults chosen against a measured ~100 ms Argon2id verification at 64 MiB and t=3. Not industry-standard guidance and not a guarantee against any particular attacker.
policies.refillBehaviour: Continuous token refill. No lockout state exists and no account can be disabled by an attacker.

enforcementModels.rationale: login and reset have credentials to guess, so charging their successes would let one shared NAT address lock out colleagues signing in correctly. forgot must meter requests because email flooding requests succeed: a failure-metered forgot would limit nothing. me and logout have no credential to fail.

trustedClientIdentity.ignoredBecauseTheyAreClientSupplied: Reading any of them would let a caller mint unlimited fresh identities with one header. No proxy is deployed to strip and rewrite them.
trustedClientIdentity.natImplication: A transport address is a network location, not a person. Every device behind one NAT shares a bucket, so one user can exhaust the source allowance for a site. Per-account and per-target meters are always applied alongside it as the mitigation.

keyPrivacy.derivation: HMAC-SHA256 over a domain-separated message, truncated to 128 bits
keyPrivacy.resetTargetSubject: SHA-256 digest of the token, which is what the token is compared by everywhere else
keyPrivacy.endpointAndDimensionInsideTheMessage: Prevents correlating one subject across endpoints from key material alone.
keyPrivacy.oversizedSubjectBounded: Truncated at 512 characters rather than rejected, so response timing does not depend on submitted length.
keyPrivacy.truncationCollisionEffect: Would merge two subjects budgets. Requires an intentional search and would at worst let one subject share another allowance, never exceed it.
keyPrivacy.ttlBounded: Every key expires after its policy window, between 60 seconds and 1 hour.
keyPrivacy.secretRotationEffect: Changes every derived key, so rotation resets every active window and fails open for up to one window.

argon2idWorkloadProtection.globalRateBudget: 120 Argon2id verifications per minute across the deployment, charged before the handler runs, unconditionally.
argon2idWorkloadProtection.chargedUnconditionally: Both an existing and a nonexistent account verify on every login by design, so the cost is paid either way.
argon2idWorkloadProtection.simultaneousVerificationEscalation: The budget bounds verification work started, not concurrent 64 MiB allocations. A genuine cap needs leases with expiry and reviewed release semantics; a half-built distributed semaphore can deadlock or double-release, so this is escalated as a real follow-up rather than claimed.

outageBehaviour.principle: Authentication protection must not silently disappear. Fail closed where protection is security-critical; keep availability where it is not.
outageBehaviour.redisUnavailableBeforeRequest: login, forgot, reset refuse with 503; me and logout proceed
outageBehaviour.redisTimeout: bounded at 750 ms, then treated as unconfirmable
outageBehaviour.redisCommandError: treated as unconfirmable; the driver message is discarded because it can contain the Redis password
outageBehaviour.malformedRedisReply: refused as unconfirmable; never treated as permission
outageBehaviour.recoveryAfterRedisHealthy: enforcement resumes immediately with state intact
outageBehaviour.multipleInstancesObservingSameOutage: every instance fails the same way, because every instance consults Redis
outageBehaviour.failClosedBehaviour: Refused before the handler, so no Argon2id is attempted and no recovery token is issued while enforcement is unconfirmed. Response is the accepted fixed 503 service_unavailable body, identical to any other service failure.
outageBehaviour.meBehaviour: Proceeds. It performs no Argon2id and issues nothing, so a Redis outage must not sign every user out.
outageBehaviour.logoutBehaviour: Proceeds and still revokes. Revocation is a PostgreSQL write in the accepted Stage 2.3 service, so Redis only ever provided the throttle. The cookie is still cleared and the 204 remains a truthful claim that the session was revoked.
outageBehaviour.circuitBreakerNote: A broad circuit-breaker platform is outside Stage 2.6 scope. A repeated Redis outage produces repeated sanitized 503s.

knownLimitations: A lease that expires while its Argon2id work is still running permits bounded over-admission. The lease is 30 s against a ~100 ms operation with renewal every 10 s, so it requires an event-loop-starved process or a pathologically slow machine.

Redis is now a hard dependency for login, password recovery, and password reset: neither the rate limiter nor the Argon2id concurrency bound can be confirmed without it, and all three endpoints fail closed. /ready already reports it.

Client identity and the trusted-origin allowlist are both not proxy-aware. Behind a TLS-terminating proxy every client shares one source bucket, and this stage is not production-ready behind such a proxy.
A refund that cannot be written is lost, so a legitimate attempt is nominally free rather than provably free under a partial outage. Bounded and self-correcting.
Per-account meters are an availability risk by nature: an attacker who knows an address can record extra failures against it. Continuous refill, no lockout.
An IPv6 client with a large address space could vary its address to obtain fresh source buckets; normalisation collapses notations of one address but not distinct addresses.
Secret rotation resets every active window, failing open for up to one window, and must keep one value across all replicas throughout.
Redis Cluster is designed for via the hash tag but was never exercised.
No circuit breaker: repeated Redis unavailability produces repeated sanitized 503s.
Rate-limit decisions and Argon2id refusals are not recorded as security events and are not alerted on. AuthenticationEvent is Stage 2.7.
deploymentBlockers: A production API_RATE_LIMIT_HMAC_SECRET must be an injected random secret shared by every replica. Per-instance values silently break distributed enforcement.
Redis availability is a hard dependency for authentication. /ready already reports Redis, so a load balancer stops routing before users see errors.
No real email provider, so password recovery remains unusable in production regardless of rate limiting.
Load-balancer policy must be decided: a TLS-terminating proxy collapses all clients onto one source bucket, and this stage is not production-ready behind one.

hardeningReview.scope: Narrowly scoped investigation and correction of two potential weaknesses: unbounded simultaneous Argon2id work, and concurrent-request bypass of failure-metered authentication policies.

findings.title: Concurrent requests could all pass admission before any failure was charged
findings.rootCause: Admission for a failure-metered endpoint was a check that wrote nothing (commit: false), and the charge happened after the handler returned. The admission decision and the charge were therefore not atomic, so N simultaneous requests all read the same untouched bucket and all proceeded.
findings.demonstratedBehaviour: Twenty concurrent failed logins were all admitted against a configured per-account allowance of 8 ({ admitted: 20, refused: 0 }). Twenty concurrent invalid reset attempts were all admitted against an allowance of 10. The same burst split across two independently created API instances was likewise fully admitted, confirming the bypass was distributed rather than per-process.
findings.previouslyDocumentedAs: A burst could overshoot by the number of requests already in flight.
findings.whyThatWasWrong: That was not a theoretical caveat but the bypass itself. Framing an unbounded number as "bounded by in-flight concurrency" made a real defect read like an accepted limitation.
findings.correctionDetail: Admission now reserves a token on every dimension atomically, so simultaneous requests contend for real state. The reservation is refunded whenever the outcome was not a credential failure, which is what keeps a legitimate attempt free. CHARGED_ERROR_CODES names the two outcomes that keep their reservation.
findings.postFixBehaviour: A burst of twenty against an allowance of eight admits at most eight, and the remainder are refused. The same holds for reset and across independently created instances.
findings.fairnessPreserved: A burst of legitimate successes at or below the allowance is admitted outright and its full budget is restored afterwards, asserted directly.

findings.title: No bound on simultaneous Argon2id allocations
findings.rootCause: A per-minute token bucket bounds work started, not work running at once. A bucket that starts full hands out its entire capacity simultaneously, so a 120-token budget permitted a 120-way burst of 64 MiB allocations. No concurrency bound existed at all.
findings.previouslyDocumentedAs: Explicitly escalated as a real follow-up rather than claimed as solved.
findings.correction: A deployment-wide leased semaphore in @tsms/redis, enforced immediately before every allocation.
findings.correctionDetail: One sorted set of lease holders. Each member is a 32-byte randomBytes holder id scored by its expiry. Acquire prunes expired members, refuses at capacity, and otherwise adds the holder; release removes only that holder and only if present; renew extends only that holder and only if present.
findings.whyARedisLeaseIsSafeHere: Every endpoint that can reach Argon2id already fails closed when Redis is unreachable, because the rate limiter is consulted first. Adding a Redis-backed admission step therefore introduces no new failure mode: if Redis is down the request was already refused before any Argon2id was attempted.
argon2idPathsCovered: login, active account with credential: verifyPassword, one slot around the whole verification
login, unknown, disabled, or no credential: decoy verifyPassword, the same slot, enumeration resistance preserved
password recovery, ineligible request: decoy verifyPassword
password recovery, eligible request: no Argon2id, and therefore no slot taken
password reset, valid token: hashPassword, slot released before the transaction opens
findings.admissionServiceRequiredWhy: Both AuthService and PasswordRecoveryService take it as a required constructor argument rather than an optional one, because omitting it would silently remove the bound.
findings.postFixBehaviour: At most 8 valid leases exist across the whole deployment at one time, shared by every API instance, verified with independently created applications and three separate Redis connections. This is a bound on valid leases, not an unconditional maximum of 8 physically running Argon2id operations: a lease that expires while its work is still running permits over-admission, bounded by the number of such holders rather than by request volume.
findings.sizingRationale: 8 concurrent operations is 512 MiB of transient allocation fleet-wide, roughly 80 verifications per second against a measured ~100 ms verification. The bound must sit above the legitimate concurrency of the product: the accepted Stage 2.5 contract includes six concurrent valid logins all being admitted, and its suite exercises six at once.
findings.residualGap: A lease that expires while its work is still running permits bounded over-admission. The lease is 30 s against a ~100 ms operation with renewal every 10 s, so it requires an event-loop-starved process or a pathologically slow machine.

argon2idConcurrency.mechanism: Redis sorted set of leased holders, one Lua script per operation
argon2idConcurrency.capacityNote: Sits above the accepted legitimate concurrency of six concurrent valid logins.
argon2idConcurrency.holderIdentity: 32 random bytes, base64url, never derived from a credential, address, or token
argon2idConcurrency.queueing: none; admission is refused immediately rather than waited on
guarantees: At most the configured number of valid leases exist across the whole deployment, and every Argon2id allocation is bracketed by a lease.
Acquisition is atomic, so concurrent acquires cannot exceed capacity.
A crashed, killed, or disconnected holder frees its slot when its lease expires; capacity never leaks permanently.
A release cannot free another holder slot, and a duplicate release cannot free two.
A renewal cannot revive a released slot.
Redis unavailability refuses admission, with no unlimited fallback.
Malformed replies and an unreadable clock are refused as unconfirmable, never treated as a granted slot.
guaranteesNotClaimed: A lease expiring while its work continues permits over-admission, bounded by the number of such holders rather than by request volume.
Redis unavailability makes login and both recovery endpoints unavailable, because neither the rate limiter nor this bound can be confirmed.
argon2idConcurrency.newHardDependency: Redis is now a hard dependency for login, password recovery, and password reset. /ready already reports it.

reservationSemantics.model: Admission reserves; the outcome refunds or keeps.
reservationSemantics.guardRefusal: Untouched. The meter refused the request and wrote nothing, so there is no reservation to return.
reservationSemantics.neverRefunded: The global verification budget, because it measures work started and returning it would undo the bound on Argon2id work.
reservationSemantics.refundFailureRationale: The response has already been produced. Losing a refund costs that caller one unit of its own allowance, and surfacing it would turn an ordinary wrong password into a 503.
reservationSemantics.successIsFreeEvidence: A test asserts a full allowance of correct sign-ins is followed by a full allowance of metered failures, which holds only if every reservation came back.
reservationSemantics.residual: A refund that cannot be written is lost, so a legitimate attempt is nominally free rather than provably free under a partial outage.

secretValidationHardened.reason: A length check alone does not establish a secret: 'x'.repeat(32) satisfies any minimum length and carries almost no entropy.
secretValidationHardened.addedRule: Reject a single repeated character or a short repeating pattern, on top of the existing length, character-class, and placeholder rules.
secretValidationHardened.deliberatelyNarrow: This is not a claim to measure entropy and cannot be. Real entropy comes from the generator that produced the value, not from inspecting it. A legitimate hex-shaped secret, which is what crypto.randomBytes(32) renders as, is explicitly accepted because rejecting it would push operators toward weaker values.
operationalPropertiesNotVerifiableByTest: shared by every replica; a per-instance value produces disjoint key spaces and silently turns a distributed limit into a per-instance one
injected by the deployment rather than committed
secretValidationHardened.rotationBehaviour: Rotation changes every derived key, so it resets every active window and fails open for up to one window.

defectsFoundDuringHardening.defect: Redis replies to TIME with bulk strings, and the semaphore read the clock assuming numbers. Every admission attempt was refused as unreadable, so login and both recovery endpoints returned 503.
defectsFoundDuringHardening.severity: A total outage of the authenticated surface.
defectsFoundDuringHardening.rootCause: Wrong assumption about the ioredis reply type.
defectsFoundDuringHardening.fix: Coerce explicitly and reject anything that is not exactly two usable components.
defectsFoundDuringHardening.foundBy: An integration run failing every login with 503. The unit test asserting an unreadable clock could not have caught it, because it supplied the numeric shape the code wrongly expected.
regressionTestsAdded: accepts the string clock Redis actually returns

defectsFoundDuringHardening.defect: An Argon2id admission refusal inside password reset was reported as a password-policy violation (400) rather than a service failure.
defectsFoundDuringHardening.severity: Conflated two distinguishable outcomes and disclosed to the client that no hashing had been attempted.
defectsFoundDuringHardening.rootCause: The guarded wrapper already converted a refusal into SERVICE_FAILURE, and the outer catch then reinterpreted that as INVALID_PASSWORD.
defectsFoundDuringHardening.fix: Re-raise an AuthError unchanged and only classify a genuine hasher failure as a policy violation.
defectsFoundDuringHardening.foundBy: The existing Stage 2.5 reset integration suite, which asserts the accepted 401 taxonomy.

defectsFoundDuringHardening.defect: The crash-recovery test for the semaphore passed even with the expiry prune removed, because the key PEXPIRE was reclaiming capacity instead of the prune.
defectsFoundDuringHardening.severity: A test that could not detect the defect it claimed to prove. Not a product defect.
defectsFoundDuringHardening.rootCause: The assertion waited for the holder set to empty, which happens either way.
defectsFoundDuringHardening.fix: The test now forces a single member expiry into the past while the key is demonstrably still present, so a reclaimed slot can only have come from the prune. It fails when the prune is removed.
defectsFoundDuringHardening.foundBy: A deliberate negative control after the first version passed with the prune deleted.

defectsFoundDuringHardening.defect: The configured Argon2id concurrency of 4 refused the excess in the accepted Stage 2.5 suite, which asserts six concurrent valid logins all succeed.
defectsFoundDuringHardening.severity: The new control broke a guarantee earlier stages established.
defectsFoundDuringHardening.rootCause: The bound was set below the product legitimate concurrency rather than above it.
defectsFoundDuringHardening.fix: Raised to 8, with the reasoning documented. The control must sit above legitimate concurrency or it becomes the outage.
defectsFoundDuringHardening.foundBy: The accepted Stage 2.5 race suite, which the hardening was required not to weaken.

negativeControls.result: PASS as a demonstration. 20 concurrent failed logins admitted 20 of 20 against an allowance of 8; after the fix the same probe is bounded.

negativeControls.result: The original test still passed, proving it was detecting the key PEXPIRE rather than the prune. After being rewritten to isolate the prune, removing it fails the test.

finalSafetyReview.scope: Documentation-independent final safety review of the reservation/refund path and the Argon2id semaphore, plus narrowly necessary Stage 2.6 corrections.
correctionsMade: Test-only: an invalid key shape in the new refund-audit suite, an unused helper, and an assertion that could have passed vacuously. No production code was changed.
refundAuditProvedAgainstRealRedis: Admission reserves atomically across every dimension and a refusal writes nothing, verified through a second dimension that is still untouched.
A 40-way concurrent burst admits exactly the capacity.
A legitimate success is refunded exactly one token and a failed credential attempt keeps its charge.
Refunds recompute refill from Redis TIME and clamp to capacity, so repeated refunds cannot inflate a bucket.
A duplicate refund cannot restore capacity twice, because the second refund saturates at capacity.
A refund cannot restore another subject budget, because keys are HMAC-derived and never caller-selectable.
A delayed refund cannot disturb a different window generation of the same key.
A refund after expiry does not resurrect the expired key.
A Redis failure during refund resolves without throwing and is never retried.
A malformed dimension is refused before the script is issued.
Keys are fixed-shape 32-character hex digests, so no raw credential, address, or Argon2id hash reaches Redis.

negativeControlAdded.method: Removed the ceiling clamp from the refund script and re-ran the refund-audit suite.
negativeControlAdded.result: Three cases failed, with buckets inflating to 8 and 12 tokens against a capacity of 5. The source was then restored and re-verified clean, and the full Redis integration suite was green on re-run twice.

semaphoreAuditFindings: Capacity of 8 valid leases, 30 s lease, 10 s renewal confirmed against the committed code.
Acquisition is atomic; holder ids are 43-character base64url values from 32 random bytes and are never derived from a credential, address, or token.
Renewal and release are both guarded by a presence check, so a delayed, duplicate, or forged release cannot free another holder's lease and a renewal cannot revive a released slot.
A crashed holder is reclaimed by the expiry prune rather than leaking capacity permanently.
All four Argon2id allocation sites are bracketed: login verification, login decoy verification, recovery decoy verification, and reset credential hashing.
Redis unavailability refuses admission with no unlimited fallback.

ownerDecisionsRecorded: Provisional Argon2id semaphore capacity of 8 is accepted.
Redis is accepted as a hard dependency for login and password recovery.
Transport-peer identity remains the authoritative client identity source.
No trusted proxy model is approved.
Production use behind a shared TLS-terminating proxy remains blocked pending architecture review.
API_RATE_LIMIT_HMAC_SECRET must be securely injected and shared by every replica.
Development thresholds remain provisional and production tuning is deferred.
remainingLimitations: Lease-expiry over-admission: a lease that expires while its work is still running permits over-admission, bounded by the number of such holders rather than by request volume. The semaphore bounds valid leases, not physically running Argon2id operations.
Redis unavailability makes login, password recovery, and password reset unavailable, because neither the rate limit nor the concurrency bound can be confirmed.
A refund that cannot be written is lost rather than queued or retried, which can under-charge a subject.

No approved trusted proxy model. Transport-peer identity collapses every client behind a shared TLS-terminating proxy onto one source bucket, which is a production blocker pending architecture review.

HMAC secret provisioning and rotation: a per-instance value produces disjoint key spaces and silently turns a distributed limit into a per-instance one, and rotation resets every active window and fails open for up to one window.
Development rate-limit thresholds are provisional; production tuning is deferred.
Redis Cluster is designed for via the hash tag but has not been exercised against a Cluster instance.
Production email delivery is not configured; password recovery still runs in its non-delivering mode.

testIsolationFix.problem: Three consecutive full-suite runs exposed intermittent failures in the Stage 2.6 hardening suites. The cause was cross-suite interference over state that is deployment-wide by design, not a defect in either control.
contributingFactors: The Argon2id semaphore is one key spanning every instance, so it is shared deployment state rather than a per-suite fixture.
apps/api and packages/redis integration suites run concurrently against the same logical Redis database, and both asserted on that shared key.
packages/redis has an accepted Stage 1 test that calls FLUSHDB on the test database, which deleted the semaphore and the rate-limit buckets out from under apps/api mid-run.

A first attempt excluded the semaphore key from the API suites cleanup. That fixed the cross-package collision but then left stale holders from earlier suites within the same package, because those run sequentially.
testIsolationFix.resolution: The root test:integration script now runs @tsms/redis first and every other package afterwards, so the FLUSHDB cannot overlap another suite. The Redis semaphore suite additionally uses its own key namespace. The API suites reset the full rate-limit namespace, including the semaphore, because they own it exclusively.
testIsolationFix.whySerializationRatherThanAFilter: Turbo cannot express a dependency from one package task onto another without also declaring it for every package, which fails with "depends on itself". Sequencing at the root script is the smallest change that is correct.
testIsolationFix.whatWasNotChanged: The FLUSHDB assertion itself is preserved unchanged; it still proves a flush is scoped to the logical database and leaves the default database intact. No production code changed. The Prisma generation task graph is unchanged.
testIsolationFix.verification: Three consecutive full pnpm test:integration runs, all green: 52 Redis, 35 database, 239 API.
